title: Expressing Disagreement, Agreement or Doubt
summary: Saying no, don't and I don't like (hindî, huwág, ayaw), yes and that's true (oô, siyangâ, totoó, talagá), and maybe (maráhil, tíla, sigúro, bakâ, maáarì)
goals: Say no with hindî and its short form dî, and know when to use walâ instead
Tell someone not to do something with huwág, using the right pronoun
Say you don't like to do something with ayaw
Agree with oô, siyangâ, totoó and talagá
Show doubt with maráhil, tíla, sigúro, bakâ and maáarì

sections.title: Words for no, yes and maybe

blocks.t: People see things differently, so everyday talk is full of **disagreeing**, **agreeing** and **doubting** (questioning whether something is true, or whether someone can do it). Tagalog has a small set of words for each of these.
Most of these words can **stand alone** as a whole answer, just like *No.*, *True.* or *Maybe.* in English.
**Hindî** means **no**. Its shortened form is **dî**. Hindî is the most common negative answer to a question, with one exception.

blocks.title: Questions with may or mayroón
blocks.t: If a question starts with **may** or **mayroón** (there is / have), the negative answer is **walâ** (none), not hindî. You met this in Lesson 12. For example, the answer to *May aklát ba kayó?* (Do you have a book?) or *Mayroón ba siyáng asawa?* (Does he have a wife?) is **walâ**.
Other questions can be answered with **hindî**, either as one word or as a full sentence:
Hindî can also be paired with short one-syllable words such as **pa** or **na** for emphasis, or it can sit inside a longer sentence.
Two ways to make a word negative
You can give a word the opposite meaning in two ways:

blocks.title: Hindî or dî
items: Put **hindî** in front of the word. The word can be a verb, an adverb, a pronoun, a noun or a *substantive* (any word or group of words that acts as a noun).
Or use the shortened form **dî**, or attach **di-** to the word as a prefix.

items.en: The child is not good. (glottal catch at the end of dî, stress at the end of mabaít)
The child is not good. (hyphen between di and mabaít; the stress is only at the end of mabaít)

blocks.t: **Huwág** means **do not, not to, not**. On its own it simply means *Don't!*, and sometimes *Stop!*. Say it whenever you want to stop something you dislike, or to warn someone not to do something.

items.en: Do you want me to beat you?

blocks.t: Huwág can stand alone, or be part of a sentence. Inside a sentence, the **kind of verb** decides which pronoun you need:

blocks.title: Which pronoun goes with huwág?
items: **Active verb** (an -um-, mag-, ma- or magpa- word): use a **personal pronoun** such as **ka**, **kayó** or **táyo**.
**Passive verb** (an -in, i- or -an word): use a **possessive pronoun** such as **mo** or **nátin**.

items.en: Don't get caught in the rain.

items.tl: Huwág mong basahan ng sulat si Ate.
items.en: Don't read my letter to Ate.

items.tl: Huwág nátin ibilí ng kendi si Jun.
items.en: Let us not buy candy for Jun.

blocks.t: Commands and requests
In a sentence that gives a **command** or makes a **request**, huwág goes with either the **infinitive** form of the verb or its **future** tense.

head: Sentence
Meaning
Kind
rows: Do not take a bath now.
Huwág mong babasahan ang batà bukas.
Do not read to the child tomorrow
blocks.title: Huwág with infinitive or future

blocks.t: **Ayaw** means **to dislike, do not like**. It is the opposite of the pseudo-verbs **gustó** (to like) and **ibig** (to like) that you met in Lesson 17. Ayaw is a **verb root**, and it shows dislike of someone or something.

It has an active form, **umayáw**, and a passive form, **ayawán**. Just like huwág, the active form needs a **personal pronoun** and the passive form needs a **possessive pronoun**. Ayaw also goes with the **infinitive** form of a verb.

head: Active (personal pronoun)
Passive (possessive pronoun)
Meaning
rows: He does not like to talk.
They do not like to go.
Don't you like to take a walk?
blocks.title: Two ways, same meaning

items.en: He does not like to talk.
He does not like to talk.
Don't you like to take a walk?

blocks.title: Ayókong
blocks.t: **Ayókong** is the joined-up form of **ayaw ako** plus the link -ng: *Ayókong kumain* = I don't like to eat.

sections.title: II. Agreement: oô, siyangâ, totoó, talagá

blocks.t: 1. Oô (yes)

**Oô** means **yes**. **Opô** and **ohô** are the polite *yes*, like *yes, sir/ma'am*. As in Lesson 3, younger people should sprinkle opô and ohô through their sentences and questions to show respect to older people, or to anyone with an honorific title or authority, whatever their age. These words show the speaker's good manners and respect for the person spoken to.

blocks.title: Who gets oô?
blocks.t: Keep **oô** for people about your own age and status. In the book's picture, a young man carrying a box answers the director with **Opô.**
2. Siyangâ (that is right, that is true)
**Siyangâ** is an **idiomatic expression** (a fixed phrase). Do not mix it up with the personal pronoun **siyá** (he/she), or the meaning changes to *It is him/her indeed*.
Use siyangâ when you **fully agree** with what someone said, or when you want someone to **confirm** something you heard from another source.

items.en: Is it true? Are you leaving?

blocks.t: 3. Totoó (true, indeed, truly)
**Totoó** as a one-word yes **confirms** a piece of information. It can answer a *Totoó?* or *Siyangâ?* question, and sometimes it can even take the place of **oô**.

items.en: Truly, he/she is not coming back anymore.

blocks.t: 4. Talagá (yes, indeed; really)

Use **talagá** to stress what the subject is like (shown by an adjective), or to confirm that a sentence is true. Like the other yes-words, it can be a whole answer by itself. Put it at the **start** of the sentence, or **near the adjective or adverb**.

items.tl: Mabuting táo talagá si G. Santos.
items.en: Mr. Santos is a really good man.

items.tl: Talágang mabuting táo si G. Santos.
items.en: Mr. Santos is a really good man.

items.tl: Talagá, papuntá kamí sa Estados Unidos.
items.en: Yes, indeed, we are going to the United States.

blocks.title: Really?
blocks.t: In casual speech talagá can also mean a doubtful *Really?*, said with **raised eyebrows** and a **rising voice** to show you don't believe it.
1. Maráhil (maybe)
**Maráhil** can also be a one-word answer. In a sentence it can go at the **beginning**, **near the subject**, or even at the **end**.

items.tl: Si Pépe na maráhil ang pinakamasuwerteng táo sa buong mundó.
items.en: Pepe maybe the luckiest person in the whole world.

items.tl: Ang pinakamasuwerteng táo sa buong mundó ay si Pépe na maráhil.
items.en: Pepe maybe the luckiest person in the whole world.

blocks.t: 2. Tíla (it seems)

A **tíla** sentence gives the speaker's own view of things. Tíla goes at the **start** of a sentence, or wherever another person's statement or view is included in the speaker's sentence (see Lesson 21).

items.en: It seems it will rain today.

blocks.t: 3. Sigúro (maybe or definitely)
As in Lesson 3, what **sigúro** means depends on the answer it is used in. The question *Sigúro ka?* (Are you sure?) can get three answers:

head: Answer
Meaning
rows: Yes, I am sure (or Yes, definitely).
blocks.title: Sigúro ka? (Are you sure?)

blocks.t: Sigúro can be a one-word answer, and it can go **anywhere** in a sentence:
4. Bakâ (might be)

There is not much difference between **maráhil**, **sigúro** (as *maybe*) and **bakâ** when you express doubt. But **bakâ** is the **most widely used**: it is the shortest, the most up to date, and the most pleasant of the three. Even so, the way a speaker says a sentence, or the words chosen, can give the opposite feel.

blocks.title: bakâ or baka?
blocks.t: Say **bakâ** with a **glottal catch** on the last syllable. The Tagalog word for **cow** is **baka**, which the book calls *stressless* here.
5. Maáarì (it can be or possible)

**Maáarìng totoó** means *it can be true*, and **maáarìng malî** means *it can be wrong*. In this way maáarì works a bit like **hindî**: hindî gives a word the opposite meaning, while maáarì puts a **blanket of doubt** over a word.
On its own as an answer, maáarì means *It is possible* (although **posible** or **puwede** are more popular). Maáarì is also used in **requests** (Lesson 24).

items.tl: Maáarìng totoó na siyá ay mag-áasawa na.
items.en: It could be true that he/she is getting married.

blocks.title: Remember
items: No: hindî (or dî / di-). After a may or mayroón question, answer walâ.
Don't: huwág + personal pronoun with active verbs (ka, kayó, táyo); + possessive pronoun with passive verbs (mo, nátin).
Don't like: ayaw, with the infinitive. Ayaw siyáng magsalitâ / Ayaw niyáng magsalitâ.
Yes: oô (peers), opô / ohô (polite). Agreeing: siyangâ, totoó, talagá.
Maybe: maráhil, tíla, sigúro, bakâ (most used), maáarì.

blocks.t: The book ends with three questions. For each one, think of **three** possible answers: one that **agrees** (sang-ayon), one that **disagrees** (dî sang-ayon) and one that shows **doubt** (álinlangan). Use the words from this lesson, such as totoó or maráhil.

items.tl: Kayó na raw ang magkasáma sa eskuweláhan ngayón?
items.en: Is it true you are now a pair in school?

items.tl: Tunay bang mahál ni Nilda si Andrew?
Gustó mo bang makilarô sa ámin?
items.en: Do you want to play with us?

Also used as the prefix di-, as in di-mabaít. The exercise page also prints di sang-ayon without the mark.

vocab.en: that is right, that is true

vocab.note: The book also writes talágang before an adjective: Talágang mabuting táo.
Not the same as baka (cow). Lesson 17 writes the cow word as báka.

exercises.q: What is the most common negative answer to a question?
exercises.explain: Hindî is the most common no.

exercises.q: How do you answer NO to "May aklát ba kayó?" (Do you have a book?)
exercises.explain: For questions starting with may or mayroón, the negative answer is walâ, not hindî.

exercises.q: What is the shortened form of hindî?
exercises.explain: Hindî is shortened to dî.

exercises.q: "Ang batà ay di-mabaít" means…
exercises.explain: di- is attached as a prefix to give the opposite meaning.

exercises.q: "Huwág!" on its own means…
exercises.explain: Huwág can also mean Stop!

exercises.q: With an ACTIVE verb (such as umalís), huwág needs…
options: a personal pronoun such as ka
a possessive pronoun such as mo
exercises.answer: a personal pronoun such as ka
exercises.explain: Huwág kang umalís. Don't leave.

exercises.q: With a PASSIVE verb (such as kanin), huwág needs…
options: a possessive pronoun such as mo
a personal pronoun such as ka
exercises.answer: a possessive pronoun such as mo
exercises.explain: Huwág mong kanin iyán. Don't eat that.

exercises.q: Fill in: Huwág ___ kanin iyán. (Don't eat that.)
exercises.explain: Kanin is passive (-in), so it takes the possessive pronoun mo.

exercises.q: "Huwág tayóng matulog" means…
exercises.explain: tayó = we (including you).

exercises.q: Ayaw is the opposite of which words?
exercises.explain: Gustó and ibig mean to like; ayaw means to dislike.

exercises.q: Which is the passive way to say "He does not like to talk"?
exercises.explain: The passive form uses a possessive pronoun: niyá.

exercises.q: "Ayókong kumain" is the joined form of…
exercises.explain: Ayókong (ayaw ako) kumain. I don't like to eat.

exercises.q: Who should you answer with plain oô?
options: People within your own age and status
exercises.answer: People within your own age and status
exercises.explain: Use opô or ohô for older people and people with titles or authority.

exercises.q: "Siyangâ, mabait siyá" means…
exercises.explain: Siyangâ shows total agreement.

exercises.q: "Totoóng-totoó" means…
exercises.explain: Totoó = true.

exercises.q: Where should talagá go in a sentence?
options: At the start, or near the adjective or adverb
Only after the subject marker ang
exercises.answer: At the start, or near the adjective or adverb
exercises.explain: Talágang mabuting táo si G. Santos.

exercises.q: Which doubt word is the most widely used?
exercises.explain: Bakâ is the shortest, most contemporary and most pleasant of the three.

exercises.q: "Tíla úulan ngayón" means…
options: It seems it will rain today.
exercises.answer: It seems it will rain today.
exercises.explain: Tíla = it seems.

exercises.q: "Maáarìng malî ang hinàla nátin" means…
exercises.explain: Maáarì puts a blanket of doubt over a word.

exercises.q: Which answer to "Sigúro ka?" means "Maybe."?
exercises.explain: Oô, sigúro akó = Yes, I am sure. Hindî akó sigúro = I am not sure.

options: that is right, that is true
exercises.explain: Huwág kang umalís. Don't leave.

options: that is right, that is true
exercises.answer: that is right, that is true
exercises.explain: Siyangâ ba? Aalís kayó?
Bakâ ka magkasakít. You might get sick.

recap: Hindî (dî, di-) = no or not. After a may or mayroón question, the no-answer is walâ.
Huwág = don't: personal pronoun with active verbs (Huwág kang umalís), possessive pronoun with passive verbs (Huwág mong kanin iyán).
Ayaw = to dislike, with the infinitive: Ayaw siyáng magsalitâ / Ayaw niyáng magsalitâ.
Agreeing: oô (opô / ohô to be polite), siyangâ, totoó, talagá.
Doubting: maráhil, tíla, sigúro, bakâ (the most used) and maáarì.
